text_to_speech: A simple circuit consists of a source of electricity, a lamp, and two wires. The lamp shines when the components are connected and the power source is turned on. If I increase the voltage, the lamp shines brighter. The power of the Electric current has also been increased. This Electric current can be determined with a measuring device. Analog amperage meters show the amperage on a scale. The video "Ameter explained" shows how these devices work. The Electric current can be read directly on a digital ammeter. But what is the Electric current? The Electric current is defined as the number of electrons that flow through a conductor's cross-section in one second. To clarify this sentence, let's take a closer look at the metal wire. A metal wire consists of immovable atomic cores (+) and movable electrons (-). This representation is simplified, it is just a model representation. The atomic nucleus move only slightly, but do not leave their place. If there is a voltage, the electrons move in the direction of the positive pole. New electrons flow in from the negative pole. The Electric current I indicates the amount of charge Q that flows through the conductor cross-section per time t. If a charge carrier flows through the conductors cross-section every second, the Electric current is 1 e per 1 s. If twice as many electrons flow through the conductors cross-section, the Electric current is twice as high. The amperage is 1 A if 6 240 000 000 000 000 000 electrons flow through the conductors cross-section in one second. That is more electrons per second than seconds have passed since the Big Bang!
